q: A dessert sweeter than the wine served with it produces which effect?
opts: The wine tastes sweeter, since the sugar carries across
The wine tastes thin and sour
The wine's fruit is lifted, as a salty dish would lift it
exp: Relative sweetness governs the perception. Out-sweetened, a wine loses its fruit and shows only acid and alcohol. Salt on the plate lifts fruit; sugar on the plate strips it, and none of the dish's sweetness transfers to the glass.

q: Which two food tastes are broadly wine-friendly, tending to make most wines taste better?
exp: Both suppress bitterness and lift fruit. It is why a squeeze of lemon or a pinch of salt can rescue a pairing that seemed wrong.

q: Which two food tastes are broadly wine-hostile?
exp: Each strips fruit and exposes structure. Both can be managed, sweetness by matching it and umami usually by adding salt.

q: Fat in a dish invites which two possible responses in the wine?
accept: acidity to cut it, or tannin to scour it
ans: Acidity to cut it, or tannin to scour it
exp: Two routes to the same end. Acidity refreshes the palate between bites; tannin binds the fat and clears it.

q: How does residual sugar in a wine interact with chilli heat?
opts: Sugar has no effect on perceived heat
Sugar makes the dish taste saltier
Sugar intensifies the burn the way alcohol does
exp: A little sweetness is the standard counter to capsaicin, which is why off-dry aromatic whites are the reflex recommendation for spicy food. It is the alcohol in a wine that drives the burn upward, never the sugar.

q: Serving a red too cold does what to its tannin and bitterness?
exp: Cold hardens tannin and sharpens bitterness while muting aroma. An over-chilled red often reads as a bad pairing when it is only a service fault.

q: Name the compound in artichoke that makes a wine tasted after it seem distortedly sweet.
exp: Cynarin interferes with the sweet receptors, so the next sip reads sweeter than it is. It is the reason artichoke has a reputation as unpairable.

q: Asparagus is difficult with wine because of which family of compounds, also prominent in Sauvignon Blanc?
exp: The green, vegetal pyrazines in the vegetable meet the same compounds in the wine and compound each other. A herbaceous Sauvignon is the usual escape rather than the problem.

q: Why is a sharply vinegar-dressed salad hard to pair?
opts: It coats the palate in fat
It is far too salty for any wine to carry
It carries more tannin than most reds
Acetic acid dominates and flattens the wine
exp: Vinegar is volatile and aggressive in a way that ordinary food acid is not, and it dominates the palate so the wine after it tastes dull. Softening the dressing is a better fix than changing the wine.

q: Faced with a fiercely hot curry, which style of wine would you pour?
exp: Sugar tempers capsaicin and low alcohol avoids feeding it. Tannin and high alcohol are the two things to avoid outright.

q: Oily fish such as mackerel with a heavily tannic red produces which specific fault?
exp: Iron in the wine reacting with the fish oils is the usual explanation. The effect is unmistakable and it is why the old white-with-fish rule persists.

q: Egg yolk is awkward with wine chiefly because of which property?
exp: A coated palate blunts everything after it. Acidity and bubbles are the usual counter, which is much of why Champagne suits egg dishes.

q: Which fortified wine is the traditional partner for dark chocolate?
accept: ruby or late bottled vintage port
exp: Chocolate's bitterness and fat need sweetness and body to stand against them. A young, fruit-forward Port has both.

q: Duck confit and haricot beans bake for hours under a crust in the French southwest, and all that fat is what the local red was built for: its Tannat tannin has more grip than a lean dish could carry. Which appellation is being poured?
exp: Tannat is among the most tannic red varieties grown in France, and the protein in the confit and the sausage binds enough of that tannin, with the fat coating the palate against what is left, for the wine to read as generous rather than punishing. Pour the same bottle beside a lean grilled fish and the tannin finds nothing to bind to, which is why this pairing only makes sense in one direction.

q: Which Loire white, especially when bottled sur lie, is the traditional match for oysters?
exp: High acid, low alcohol, no oak and a faint saline lees character. It is close to a neutral frame around the oyster.

q: Sauternes with foie gras is chiefly an example of which strategy?
opts: A deliberate mismatch of weight and intensity
Tannin binding with the liver's protein
Contrast, a dry wine cutting the fat
exp: The pairing works by matching opulence with opulence, the wine's sweetness and weight meeting the richness of the liver, with its acidity keeping the combination from cloying. Nothing here is dry and nothing here is tannic.
